methodology.heading: Methodology
methodology.p1: The data come from the monthly lists published by the National Health Insurance Fund of Hungary (NEAK): vacant dental and GP services, vacant dental services with terminated contracts, and the registries of contracted providers. NEAK's data are informative in nature and reflect the monthly financing-contract status — they are not real-time operational data.
methodology.p2: A district is “vacant” when it has no contracted physician. This is not the same as “unserved”: residents of vacant districts are covered by a substitute physician. The “terminated contract” category marks dental districts whose financing contract has also ended — NEAK publishes no such list for the GP branch. Long-term vacancy is a legal category: under Government Decree 313/2011 (XII. 23.) it applies to districts where at least 6 months have passed since the contract ended.
methodology.p3: The denominator of the vacancy rate is the number of unique primary-care district codes (FIN or HSZ) in NEAK's registries. On the dental branch adult, paediatric, mixed and school-youth services count (on-call and university services and specialist care do not); on the GP branch, districts with a territorial care obligation (T) — practices without one (TN) are excluded, as they cannot appear on the vacancy list either.
methodology.p4: Practice coordinates are determined with OpenStreetMap's Nominatim service. Where an address could not be identified precisely, the settlement centre is marked and flagged on the map. District boundaries are not officially published, so the map colours at county level and shows districts as points.
methodology.p5: On the GP branch the settlement search is based on the official list of settlements served by each district, so small villages can also be found; the dental registry only records the practice seat, so there the search covers the practices' settlements and the settlements served by terminated districts.
methodology.p6: The full processing code and every month's raw source file are public in the project repository — every number can be traced back to its original source. The contracted physician's name of a filled practice is shown from NEAK's public contracted-provider database; we never publish a personal name for a vacant or terminated district or for a substitute physician.
methodology.p7: The per-capita indicators (share of population living in a vacant district; districts per 10,000 residents; settlement populations) use the resident population of the HCSO Gazetteer as of 1 January 2025. This single edition is applied to every archived month — for historical months this is an approximation, noted here. Settlements are identified by HCSO code and settlement name; Budapest's districts are counted separately.
methodology.p8: The legal category of long-term vacant districts is taken from the continuously updated lists of the OKFŐ Primary Care Directorate (alapellatas.okfo.gov.hu). The list carries no NEAK code, so matching uses the settlement, the service type and the starting month of the vacancy; the list's as-of date is shown in the interface. The flag applies to the current month and is not applied retroactively to historical months.
methodology.embedText: The map can be embedded in any page with the code below (parameter k: dental or gp; optional parameter m: county name):
methodology.p9: The EESZT supplement (source H) is built from three public registers of the EESZT master-data publication: NEAK_FINSZOLG (financed services), EUSZOLG_PUBLIKUS (healthcare providers) and EUSZOLG_ENGEDELY_PUBLIKUS (operating licences). Matching uses official codes only: from the NEAK FIN code through the organisational-unit code to the licence of the district's own profession (GP 6301–6303, dental 1300/1304/1305). We check whether the licensed premises lie in the district's settlement and whether the licensee's tax number matches the financed provider; differences are flagged, and where a FIN points to several licences at different premises no premises are shown. The district number is extracted from the official service name with a strict pattern. The provider name is shown only for filled districts; for vacant districts no free-text name field is taken over, as organisational-unit names often carry the former physician's name. On the EESZT map each district is drawn at its licensed premises; addresses are geocoded with OpenStreetMap Nominatim (at most 1 request per second, cached). Where an address cannot be resolved at street level, the settlement centre is used — shown as a fainter point on the map and in the "approximate location" column; districts without coordinates are not drawn.

why.heading: Why does primary care matter?
why.lead: The GP, the paediatrician and the dentist are the gateway to healthcare: they are the first to see a complaint, they know the family, the medical history, the everyday life of the settlement. Primary care is not “minor medicine” — it is the level where a large share of diseases can be prevented or caught in time.

gp.title: General practitioner
gp.text: Managing chronic diseases — hypertension, diabetes —, organising screenings, vaccinations, and the first examination that decides whether specialist care is needed. Where a district is unfilled, all of this is squeezed into a substitute's reduced consulting hours.

ped.title: Paediatrician
ped.text: Age-linked status examinations, the vaccination schedule and monitoring development are the basis of recognising childhood diseases early. Vacancies in paediatric districts affect the youngest — see them on the map with the “paediatric” type filter.

dental.title: Dentist
dental.text: Caries and periodontal disease are preventable, and early detection of oral cancer can save lives — all of which depends on regular dental screening. In a vacant district the population typically only has local access to emergency care: prevention is the first thing to fall away.

why.chainIntro: Switch between what happens to the same patient with and without a filled district:
why.dataTie: Today {gpPop} people in Hungary live in a vacant GP district and {dentalPop} in a vacant dental district — for them this chain is not a given.
why.disclaimer: The relationships above are general public-health knowledge; we make numerical claims only from our own, sourced data.
chainOkDesc: The district has a doctor: complaints are not left unanswered, examination is available locally.
At regular screening even a still symptomless change comes to light in time.
A disease found early is simpler to treat: medication, care, follow-up.
The complication never happens — the patient lives their life, the hospital never enters the picture.
chainBrokenDesc: The district has no doctor: the practice is closed, substitution is available elsewhere and less often.
Screenings are missed — for those who cannot reach a doctor, nobody looks for anything.
The symptomless change grows quietly and surfaces late, with complaints.
A late diagnosis means more serious intervention and longer, costlier care.
chainOkDentalDesc: The district has a dentist: complaints and the annual check-up are both available locally, in time.
At screening even tiny, symptomless decay comes to light in time.
Decay found early is simple to treat: one small filling and done.
The teeth stay sound — with regular check-ups, major intervention never enters the picture.
chainBrokenDentalDesc: The district has no dentist: the practice is closed, locally only emergency care is available at best.
Screenings are missed — nobody notices the tiny decay.
Decay spreads quietly and announces itself with pain and swelling.
A tooth beyond saving must be extracted — replacement is longer, more painful and far more expensive.

eesztInfo.title: How we matched the EESZT data
eesztInfo.subtitle: EESZT download: {asOf} · NEAK data: {month} · every step is traceable
eesztInfo.p1: The map is built on NEAK's monthly vacancy lists and contracted-provider registry; these define the districts and their FIN codes. The EESZT supplement adds no districts. It only attaches further official public data to existing districts: the district number, the licensed premises, on-call participation, public funding, and for filled districts the financed provider. Whatever cannot be linked unambiguously is not shown, and we give the reason.
eesztInfo.regFinszolg: Services financed by NEAK: FIN code (FINKOD), organisational-unit code (NNGYK9_KOD), service type (TIP), official service name (FINNEV), provider name (INEV), institution code (INTKOD) and the first 8 digits of the provider's tax number (ADOIGSZ_8).
eesztInfo.regEuszolg: Register of healthcare providers: provider id (EUSZOLG_AZONOSITO), name, tax number, seat.
eesztInfo.regEngedely: Operating licences: licence id, organisational-unit code (SZERVEZETI_EGYSEG_KOD), provider id, premises address, profession (SZAKMA_KOD), public funding (KOZFINANSZIROZOTT) and on-call participation.
eesztInfo.p2: The link in the first column opens the register on the public EESZT portal. The raw download is archived unchanged in the project repository, so it can be re-run and checked at any time.
eesztInfo.p3a: The EESZT master-data page loads its data from a public REST endpoint. We used the same endpoint, paging with 500 rows per page:
eesztInfo.p3b: Each download checks that the number of rows received exactly matches the total the server reports (totalRowCount), that there are no duplicate rows, and that the total did not change during the download. If any check fails, the download stops with an error and no data is taken over. The download code:
eesztInfo.s1: Starting point: every district in NEAK's latest monthly data (filled, vacant, terminated) with its FIN code.
eesztInfo.s2: FIN code → NEAK_FINSZOLG: looked up in the FINKOD field. Only rows of the branch's own type are used: TIP = FOG for dental, TIP = HSZ for GP. A FIN code can appear in several rows (several organisational units); all of them are kept.
eesztInfo.s3: NEAK_FINSZOLG.NNGYK9_KOD → EUSZOLG_ENGEDELY_PUBLIKUS.SZERVEZETI_EGYSEG_KOD: the unit's operating licences are found by exact match on the unit code.
eesztInfo.s4: Profession filter: only licences for the district's own profession are accepted. GP: 6301 general practice, 6302 paediatric general practice, 6303 mixed general practice. Dental: 1300 dental care, 1304 paediatric dentistry, 1305 school dentistry.
eesztInfo.s5: Choosing the licence: if there are several, we take the one whose premises lie in the district's NEAK settlement and that names an actual address.
eesztInfo.s6: Provider check: the licence's EUSZOLG_AZONOSITO leads to the provider in EUSZOLG_PUBLIKUS, whose tax number (first 8 digits) is compared with NEAK_FINSZOLG.ADOIGSZ_8.
eesztInfo.p4: Every link rests on an exact match of official codes. No name-based or similarity (fuzzy) matching is used anywhere. The matching code:
eesztInfo.c1: if a FIN code belongs to several organisational units whose licences name different addresses, we do not pick one: no premises are shown for that district, and it appears among the unmatched with the reason "ambiguous".
eesztInfo.c2: if the licensed premises lie in another settlement than the district's NEAK seat, the premises are shown but flagged ("differs from the district's NEAK seat"). "Budapest" and "Budapest VIII. kerület" are treated as matching.
eesztInfo.c3: whether the licensee's and the financed provider's tax numbers match is shown in its own column ("Tax number matches").
eesztInfo.c4: the district number and provider name are shown only when every row of a FIN code carries the same value.
eesztInfo.c5: every district falls into exactly one category: it either has a matched licence or a recorded reason why not. The build stops if matched plus unmatched districts do not add up to the total.
eesztInfo.n1: The financed provider name and institution code are shown only for filled districts (the contracted provider NEAK itself publishes).
eesztInfo.n2: For vacant and terminated districts no free-text name field is taken over: organisational-unit names often carry the former physician's name ({n} such vacant districts in the current data; their names are not published).
eesztInfo.n3: Of the trace codes, the provider id is also given only for filled districts; the other codes (organisational unit, licence) carry no personal data.
eesztInfo.n4: The build checks these rules automatically and stops on any violation; tests protect them as well.
eesztInfo.p7: The official service name (FINNEV) is free text, so we extract only the district number, with a strict pattern. For example "Tatabánya 8. sz. gyermek körzet." → "8. gyermek körzet", "BETÖLTETLEN - 1. körzet, Beremend" → "1. körzet". If the pattern is not unambiguous, or the result contains a personal-name marker, no district number is shown.
eesztInfo.p8: Licensed premises addresses are geocoded with OpenStreetMap Nominatim, at most 1 request per second, cached. We first search at street level with the postcode, then without it. If neither returns a result, the settlement centre is used, shown as a fainter point on the map and in the "Approximate location" column. Districts without coordinates are not drawn. The geocoding code:
eesztInfo.p9: Percentages refer to the total number of districts. The list of unmatched districts, with reasons, is available in the table marked with the warning icon, filterable and exportable.

eesztInfo.p10: The Sásd dental district (vacant), step by step. Each link opens, on the public EESZT portal, exactly the row the data was taken from.
eesztInfo.e1: NEAK FIN code: {fin}. In NEAK_FINSZOLG it has one row of type FOG.
eesztInfo.e2: In that row the organisational-unit code (NNGYK9_KOD) is {unit}.
eesztInfo.e3: The unit's dental operating licence: {licence}; premises: {address}; profession: {profession}.
eesztInfo.e4: Check: premises in the district's settlement: {settlement}; licensee's tax number matches the financed provider: {provider}.
eesztInfo.e5: Because the district is vacant, no provider name or provider id is published; the premises, on-call duty and public funding are shown.
eesztInfo.h11: How can you verify it yourself?
eesztInfo.v1: Click any point on the map: the "Trace" part of the side panel links to the EESZT portal — FIN code, organisational unit, licence, and for filled districts the provider.
eesztInfo.v2: In the full table, the "Organisational unit code", "Licence id" and "Provider id" columns can be switched on from the "Columns" menu; they link to EESZT too.
eesztInfo.v3: The filtered table can be exported as CSV or TSV and compared with the source in bulk.
eesztInfo.v4: The raw download, the download code and the matching code are public in the project repository; running them on the same download gives the same result.
eesztInfo.l1: EESZT data reflects the day of download, NEAK data the month; the two may differ (e.g. a freshly filled district).
eesztInfo.l2: The licensed premises are not necessarily the actual consulting place, and one licence may cover several districts (see the "Shared organisational unit" column).
eesztInfo.l3: The district number appears only where the official name contains it unambiguously.
eesztInfo.l4: Points at a settlement centre indicate an approximate location only.

svc.s1: From the NEAK contracted dental provider list we take the {what}. District services are not included here — the other tab describes those.
svc.s2: The service's unit code is looked up in the EESZT financed-services register (NEAK_FINSZOLG), filtered to the FOG (dental) service type.
svc.s3: From that row we read the organisational unit's NNGYK9 code and use it to find the operating licences in the licence register (EUSZOLG_ENGEDELY_PUBLIKUS).
svc.s4: Of those licences we accept only the one issued for the service's own profession ({professions}).
svc.s5: From the licence we take the premises, the profession code, the public funding flag and the on-call participation; the provider's tax number is cross-checked against the financing register.
svc.s6: If the code points at several units whose licences disagree on the premises, we pick none: the service goes on the “unmatched” list with its reason.
svc.c1: A licence counts only with the profession code that belongs to the service type ({professions}). A licence for something else does not prove the service operates there.
svc.c2t: No pick when it is ambiguous
svc.c2: With several units and several different premises we assign none, and show what the candidates were instead.
svc.c3t: A licence that names its premises wins
svc.c3: Among candidate licences we take the one that names its premises and sits in the settlement NEAK gives.
svc.c4: The licensee's tax number is compared with the financing register's; the result is a column of its own and never changes the match.
svc.n1: NEAK itself publishes the physicians in the contracted-provider list, so they are shown — for on-call services the whole roster, as the list gives it.
svc.n2: The provider name, NEAK code and EESZT provider id are carried only where the list also names a contracted physician; {n} services name none, and there these fields stay empty.
svc.n3: The build checks this automatically and stops on a violation; tests guard it too.
svc.p7: A specialist unit code is not a FIN code: it can contain a letter (02006A425, for example), so a 9-character alphanumeric code is expected — nothing is dropped silently. For on-call services the list gives one row per physician, so one code has many rows; they are merged into one service and the row count is kept.
svc.p8: The map location is the EESZT licensed premises where there is a match, and the NEAK surgery address otherwise. The table's “source of the map location” column always says which. Geocoding is the same cached Nominatim process:
svc.p9: The highlighted numbers open the affected services as a filterable, exportable table; for the ambiguous cases every candidate licence is listed row by row.

svc.e1: In the NEAK list, the {type} service with code {code} ({settlement}).
svc.e2: In the financing register it belongs to organisational unit {unit}.
svc.e3: That unit's licence for the profession: {licence} — {profession}, premises: {address}.
svc.e4: Does the premises settlement match NEAK's: {settlementMatch}. Does the provider tax number match: {providerMatch}.
svc.v1: Every code is a link: clicking it in the table opens exactly that row on the public EESZT portal.
svc.v2: The raw EESZT files and the NEAK provider list are both in the repository, with their dates — any number can be recomputed.
svc.v3: The ETL recomputes every number from the raw files; if the row counts disagree, or a service is neither matched nor explained, the build fails.
svc.l1: These services are not districts: they count towards neither the district total nor the vacancy rate.
svc.l2: The NEAK list is indicative and lags changes made during the month.
svc.l3: The licence register shows the operating licence, not opening hours: a licence does not mean the {what} are available right now.

xc.s1: We take the NEAK records the code chain could not pair with an EESZT licence — districts and services alike.
xc.s2: The NEAK surgery address is normalized (accents folded, abbreviations expanded: u. → utca, krt → körút, house number extracted, Budapest districts unified), and so is every premises address in the licence register. An exact agreement in the record's own profession family is a first-tier hit.
xc.s3: The two registers often spell the same address differently (“Semmelweis I. u. 1.” ↔ “Semmelweis utca 1.”), so a second pass compares the street's stem, its type and the house number, ignoring abbreviated forenames and “Dr.” prefixes. “Kossuth tér” still differs from “Kossuth utca”.
xc.s4: Where the address leads nowhere we use the provider's tax number: the financing register's tax field is matched against the provider register, and we check whether that provider holds a licence of the right profession in the settlement. This is a deterministic link, not a similarity.
xc.s5: Finally the weaker evidence: the same street at another house number, then a provider-name match (legal forms — Kft., Korlátolt Felelősségű Társaság — and generic words removed, from 60% overlap).
xc.c1t: A suggestion is not a pairing
xc.c1: Nothing from the cross-check enters the district data: it never changes a match and never counts towards the coverage numbers. It is a separate table with its own reasoning.
xc.c2: A dental district only matches a dental licence (13xx), a GP district a GP one (63xx). If the address holds only another profession's licence, that is reported as its own result.
xc.c3: A column states whether the hit came from the premises address, the street name or the provider name, and a full sentence explains it.
xc.c4t: The name policy holds here too
xc.c4: Free-text names appear only where NEAK itself publishes a contracted physician; everywhere else the output carries codes, addresses and profession names only.
xc.names: The cross-check follows the same name rules as the rest: the free-text names of organisational units and premises are never exported, because they often carry a physician's name. The suggestions rest on codes, addresses and profession names.
xc.rEesztOnly: Services that exist in EESZT only
xc.p9: Clicking a number lists every candidate row by row (unit, licence id, premises, profession), filterable and exportable.
xc.l1: An address match is not proof: several services can share a building, and a mistyped address can produce an accidental hit.
xc.l2: A provider-name match is the weakest evidence: a rename or a similarly named company can mislead.
xc.l3: The “in EESZT only” list is not necessarily a missing district: it can be an on-call, school or other service the published NEAK lists do not carry.
xc.drillSubtitle: Every candidate row by row — {kind} records
xc.s6: The other direction is checked too: which dental and GP services appear in the EESZT financed-services register while the published NEAK lists do not contain them — those are also compared with the earlier monthly NEAK snapshots.
xc.c5: A health centre can hold ten or twenty surgeries at the same address, so candidates are ranked by strength: the one the provider's tax number confirms comes first, then the exact address match. The table flags the tax agreement in a column of its own.

neak.title: The district in the NEAK registry
neak.notFound: No filled record for this district in the NEAK list.
neak.source: Source: NEAK contracted-provider list, {month}. The data is indicative.

extra.oncallExplain: Contracted dental on-call services on the primary-care level. The NEAK list names every physician on the duty roster on its own row, so one service has several registry rows. These are not districts and never enter the vacancy rate.
extra.universityExplain: Dental primary care run by the university clinics. They carry no territorial obligation, so they stay out of the district denominator.
extra.specialistExplain: Every contracted dental specialist service: oral surgery, orthodontics, radiology, periodontology, paediatric and university specialist care, and care for people with disabilities. The join is the one used above, with the EESZT profession code that belongs to the service type (radiology → 1306, for example).
extra.tableSubtitle: NEAK contracted-provider list, {month} · EESZT as of {asOf}
extra.note: Source: the NEAK contracted dental provider list ({month}) and the EESZT master publication ({asOf}). These services are not districts: they count towards neither the district total nor the vacancy rate.
extra.unmatchedSubtitle: Services with no unambiguous EESZT licence — with the reason

why.noUnitLicence: The service's organisational unit ({units}) holds no licence for its own profession in the EESZT licence register.
why.noFin: The service's code does not appear in the EESZT financed-services register as a dental (FOG) service.

crosscheck.explain: Where the code chain (FIN → organisational unit → licence) found nothing, we look from the other side: is the same surgery or the same provider in EESZT after all — possibly under a different organisational unit? Addresses and names are compared in normalized form (accents, abbreviations, house number), and every row states what the hit is based on. These are suggestions, not official pairings.
crosscheck.summary: {n} of {total} records ({share}) got a usable pairing suggestion.
crosscheck.note: The comparison runs between the NEAK contracted-provider list, the EESZT financed-services register, the provider register and the licence register, as of {asOf}.
crosscheck.tableSubtitle: The best suggestion per record, with its reasoning · EESZT as of {asOf}
crosscheck.eesztOnlySubtitle: Financed {kind} services in EESZT that the published NEAK lists do not contain · {asOf}

verdict.otherProfessionAtAddress: Only another profession at the address

why.otherUnit: At the surgery address NEAK gives, EESZT holds a {profession} licence ({place}) — but under organisational unit {unit}, not the record's own ({own}). Most likely the same surgery, filed under a different unit.
why.ownUnit: At this address the record's own unit ({unit}) does hold a {profession} licence; the automatic join rejected it because of “{reason}” — worth checking by hand.
why.otherProfession: There is an EESZT licence at the address, but for another profession ({professions}); no {kind} licence was found there.
why.street: The same street has a {profession} licence ({place}) at a different house number — a spelling difference or the neighbouring building.
why.provider: The provider name matches an EESZT provider by {overlap}, and that provider holds a {profession} licence in the settlement ({unit}) — but the addresses differ.
why.noneInSettlement: The settlement has {n} same-profession EESZT licences, none of them at the NEAK address or street; the provider name gave no hit either.
why.noneAtAll: The settlement has no same-profession EESZT licence at all — the surgery cannot be identified by address or by name.
why.otherUnitTax: At the surgery address NEAK gives there is a {profession} licence ({place}) under unit {unit}, and the provider's tax number confirms it: the financing register's number equals the licensee's. The record's own unit ({own}) holds no licence — this is the most likely pairing.
why.otherUnitLoose: The same address holds a {profession} licence ({place}) under unit {unit}, not the record's own ({own}). The two registers spell the address differently (NEAK: {neak}), so the match rests on the street's stem, its type and the house number.
why.tax: The addresses differ, but by the tax number in the financing register the same provider holds a {profession} licence in the settlement ({unit}, {place}). That is a deterministic link, not a similar name.

crosscheck.manualTitle: Districts that need a human decision
crosscheck.manualSubtitle: Their own organisational unit does hold a licence at the NEAK address, yet no automatic pairing was made
crosscheck.colWhy: Why the automation did not choose
crosscheck.colInArchive: Was in an earlier NEAK list

manual.why: The code belongs to {units} organisational units with {places} different premises, so the ambiguity rule made the automatic join pick none of them.
manual.pick: At the district's headquarters address ({address}) its own unit {unit} holds a {profession} licence: {licence}. The other {n} licences are the same service's surgeries in other settlements. Recommended pairing: {licence}.
manual.decide: Several licences sit at the NEAK address — a human decision is needed.

history.found: It was in earlier NEAK lists: {months} archived months between {first} and {last}, last seen as “{status}” ({settlement}). Most likely the remnant of a discontinued district that EESZT still lists as financed.
history.never: It has never appeared in an archived NEAK list since {from} — probably not a territorial district (it may be an on-call, school or institutional service).

access.heading: How far is the nearest surgery?
access.explain: For every {kind} district with no contracted physician we measure how far the nearest surgery with a contracted physician is (as the crow flies, from the district's headquarters address). The distance approximates access: it does not say the district is unserved — substitution is invisible in the published data, and a straight line is not travel time.
access.median: median distance to the nearest operating surgery from {kind} districts without a contracted physician
access.sameSettlementShare: of the districts find an operating surgery in the same settlement
access.beyond10: people live in a district whose nearest surgery is beyond 10 km
access.tableTitle: Distance to the nearest operating surgery — {kind} districts
access.tableSubtitle: Districts without a contracted physician, with crow-flies distance · filterable, exportable
access.colNearest: Settlement of the nearest operating surgery
access.colNearestId: FIN code of the nearest district
access.note: The calculation rests on {operating} operating surgeries from the {month} list; {missing} filled districts had no coordinates and were left out, so the distances err on the high side. The distance is a straight line, not a route; substitution does not appear in the published data.
access.countyTableSubtitle: Mean and median distance to the nearest operating surgery, per county · filterable, exportable
access.countyLine: {county}: {districts} districts without a contracted physician · mean {mean} km · median {median} km · longest {max} km · {within5} within 5 km, {beyond10} beyond 10 km ({people} residents).

data.heading: Data and downloads
data.explain: Every number on this site comes from these files, and all of them are downloadable. Use them freely; the source data is published by NEAK, EESZT, KSH and OpenStreetMap, and the processing code is MIT-licensed.

file.latest_json: The latest monthly snapshot for both branches: vacant and dissolved districts with address, coordinates and population, plus the filled districts from the NEAK registry.
file.timeseries_json: Monthly series from 2017: vacant and dissolved districts and affected population, by county.
file.history_json: Per-district history from the archived months (when it was vacant).
file.months: Every archived monthly snapshot, per branch.
file.eeszt_json: The EESZT match per district: operating licence, premises, profession, public funding, on-call, trace codes, coordinates, and the unmatched cases with their reason.
file.dental_extra_json: The dental services that are not districts: on-call, university primary care and all specialist care, with their EESZT match.
file.crosscheck_json: Cross-check: address- and name-based suggestions for the records the code chain could not pair, plus the services that exist in EESZT only.
file.access_json: Distance to the nearest operating surgery from every district without a contracted physician.
file.cities_geojson: City points by rank: county seat, county-rank city, district seat, town above 20 000 residents.
file.providers_json: Unified provider list: NEAK code and name, official company name, tax number, seat and the provider's whole portfolio.
file.operating_json: Operating level: the licence, organisational unit and premises per praxis.
file.kedvezmenyezett_json: Beneficiary settlements under annexes 2 and 3 of 105/2015. (IV. 23.) Korm. rendelet (socio-economic, unemployment and temporary status).
file.vedono_json: Health-visitor services (EESZT): territorial and school districts, operators, premises
file.specialist_json: Inpatient and outpatient specialist institutions (NEAK): departments, rooms, professions, sites
file.risk_json: Vacancy risk: the 12-month probability for every filled district and the multipliers behind it
file.survival_json: Survival analysis: every vacancy spell and the Kaplan–Meier curves
file.coverage_json: Settlement coverage: every settlement's state, read at settlement level instead of district seats
file.composite_json: Composite care-risk index per settlement, broken into its components
file.age_json: Age composition per settlement (KSH, 2022 census, CC BY 4.0)
file.settlements_geojson: Settlement centres (OpenStreetMap) with KSH code and population
file.emergency_json: On-call and emergency points (EESZT) with the distances measured from them per settlement
file.workforce_json: Physician changes from the archive and the physicians holding several districts (no names, pseudonymous keys)
file.clusters_json: Contiguous care deserts and their settlements
file.traveltime_json: Driving minutes from every settlement to the nearest care point (OpenStreetMap roads)
file.transit_json: Public-transport reach: departures and direct services to where care is (Volánbusz GTFS)

data.use1: The files are static and versioned: a finished month stays in months/, while latest.json always points at the current one.
data.use2: Every number traces back to a raw source file archived in the repository with its date — the git history is the audit trail.
data.use3: When you cite it, please name the original source (NEAK / EESZT publication, as-of date) and note that the data is indicative.
data.rawArchive: raw source files in the repository

providers.explain: One row per contracted provider. The NEAK list identifies them by a short trade name and a NEAK code; the official company name, the tax number and the registered seat come from the EESZT provider register, and the tax number in the financing register links the two. The result shows in one place who runs what: how many dental and GP districts, on-call and specialist services, in how many settlements.
providers.identified: providers identified in the EESZT provider register
providers.tableSubtitle: NEAK code and name, official company name, tax number, seat and portfolio · EESZT as of {asOf}
providers.note: The list holds only providers NEAK itself publishes (through a service where the registry names the contracted physician). The official name and the seat come from the EESZT provider register ({asOf}); company officers appear in none of the registers used here, so they are not shown.

operating.explain: One row per praxis: the operating licence it works under, in which organisational unit and at which premises. The licence comes from the code chain where that worked; where it did not, the cross-check's accepted suggestion fills in (including the eleven districts whose own unit holds the licence at their headquarters address). Dissolved and vacant districts are absent: with no contracted physician there is no operating licence to assign.
operating.multiSite: praxes with premises in more than one place
operating.tableTitle: Operating level — praxes and their operating licences
operating.tableSubtitle: Only praxes with a contracted physician · EESZT as of {asOf}
operating.note: Dissolved and vacant districts are left out on purpose. Where a praxis has several organisational units and premises, every NNGYK9 is printed with its own address. Where no usable licence was found the field reads “NINCS TALÁLAT”.
operating.colProvider: Healthcare provider (name in the company register)
operating.colFinUnits: Organisational unit(s) per the financing register

benefit.compareExplain: The same districts in two groups: those whose seat is a beneficiary settlement under 105/2015. (IV. 23.) Korm. rendelet, and those whose is not. The distance is the same measure as above: a straight line to the nearest operating surgery.
benefit.source: Source: annexes 2 and 3 of 105/2015. (IV. 23.) Korm. rendelet (Nemzeti Jogszabálytár), matched by the settlement name and county the decree uses.
benefit.groupSubtitle: The districts of this group — filterable, sortable, exportable

risk.heading: Vacancy risk
risk.explain: Every {kind} district with a doctor today, ranked by how likely it is to go vacant within {horizon} months. The model learned from the archived monthly NEAK snapshots ({months} complete months since {from}): it measured the actual transition rates behind each characteristic. It is transparent, not a black box — every row states what pushed its own number up or down.
risk.baseRate: the chance that an average {kind} district goes vacant within {horizon} months
risk.checkExplain: The model was fitted on the months before {from} and used to rank what happened afterwards: {events} real vacancies. In the decile it marked riskiest, {top} went vacant against {base} on average — a {lift}× hit rate (AUC {auc}). Good for ranking, not for individual prediction.
risk.tableSubtitle: Chance of going vacant within {horizon} months · filterable, exportable
risk.countySubtitle: How many districts fall into the two riskiest bands
risk.factorsExplain: The multipliers are not assumptions but rates measured in the archive: how much more (or less) often a district went vacant with that characteristic. The events column is the number of observed vacancies, the last one the raw 12-month rate.
risk.l1: This is a ranking, not a prediction: it says where to look first, not whether a given doctor will leave.
risk.l2: The archived months are unevenly spaced (1–14 months apart), so transitions are converted to monthly exposure.
risk.l3: The model cannot see the physician's age — the most important missing factor; "same physician for X years" only approximates it.
risk.l4: Provider size and neighbouring vacancies are taken from today's state; every other characteristic uses only its own past in each month.
risk.note: Data as of {month}. No physician's name leaves the pipeline — the tenure factor appears only as a duration.

analysis.heading: Analysis
analysis.lead: What lies beyond the monthly snapshot: which district may lose its doctor, how long districts have lasted so far, how much of the country is actually covered at settlement level, and where several problems meet at once.

vedono.label: Health-visitor districts
vedono.heading: Health-visitor districts
vedono.explain: The third branch of primary care: {services} financed health-visitor services — {territorial} territorial and {school} school ones. Since the 2023 state takeover they are run mostly by county hospitals; this shows how many districts each operator holds and where the premises are.
vedono.noVacancy: This section does not speak about vacancies: neither NEAK nor OKFŐ publishes a vacancy list for health-visitor districts — what is public is the EESZT master publication (financed services and operating licences). So what you see here is the number of services, their operators and premises, not whether a health visitor is currently working in a given district.
vedono.loadTitle: How much load falls on one territorial district?
vedono.loadExplain: Under decree 49/2004. (V. 21.) ESZCSM a territorial health-visitor district is built around some 250 children under seven, which is roughly {reference} residents. The breakdown below shows how many counties fall below, around or above that — resident count only approximates the number of children, it does not replace it.
vedono.tableSubtitle: Every financed territorial and school health-visitor service · filterable, exportable
vedono.countySubtitle: Service counts and residents per territorial service
vedono.providerSubtitle: How many districts each provider holds
vedono.uncoveredSubtitle: No registered health-visitor premises here — which does not mean no health visitor comes
vedono.coveredSubtitle: At least one health-visitor service has registered premises here
vedono.note: Source: EESZT master publication, {asOf}. An operating licence was found for {licence} services and not for {missing}. Geocoded premises: {geocoded}. No health visitor's name appears anywhere.

specialist.heading: Specialist institutions
specialist.lead: The inpatient and outpatient specialist institutions contracted by NEAK — from the same NEAK directory the district registries come from.
specialist.explain: Primary care ends where these begin: none of these rows ever enters a vacancy rate. But this is the network a GP or dentist refers patients into, so it is worth seeing what is available where, and how rare some professions are.
specialist.professionsExplain: A profession existing in the country does not mean it is available everywhere. The bars show how many of the national profession list are present in each county — for the missing ones the patient travels. Professions are matched by NEAK code, not by name, because the two lists spell them differently.
specialist.coverageLine: {care}: {total} professions on the list. The most — {bestN} — are available in {best}, the fewest in {worst}: {worstN}.
specialist.siteSubtitle: One row per site · filterable, exportable, mappable
specialist.rowSubtitle: Every department and consulting room by profession, as NEAK publishes it
specialist.institutionSubtitle: How many units, professions and sites each institution holds
specialist.countySubtitle: Institutions, departments, rooms and residents per room
specialist.professionSubtitle: In how many units, institutions and counties each is present
specialist.rareSubtitle: Professions present in at most three counties, with those counties listed
specialist.coverageSubtitle: How many national professions are present in the county and how many are missing
specialist.note: Source: NEAK contracted providers, {month}. {rows} rows in total, {geocoded} of them with a geocoded site.
specialist.pdfNote: Both lists are parsed from the XLSX files: the PDF of the outpatient list stops 84 rows before the end of its own sheet, so it cannot serve as a complete source.

survival.heading: Survival analysis: how long does a vacancy last?
survival.explain: How many districts are vacant today cannot tell a three-month handover from a ten-year hole. The archive can: every monthly snapshot since {from} names the {kind} districts without a physician, so every vacancy can be followed. {spells} vacancy spells in total, {refilled} of which ended with a district being filled again and {open} still running. The curve is a Kaplan–Meier estimate: the share of vacancies still open after N months — spells that are still running are kept as censored rather than dropped.
survival.tableSubtitle: The start, end and length of every spell in the archive
survival.note: The archived months are unevenly spaced ({min}–{max} months, median {median}), so a spell's length is measured between archived months, not to the day. {truncated} spells were already running in the first archived month, so their true length is longer than shown.

coverage.heading: Settlement coverage instead of district seats
coverage.explain: Vacancies are counted where the {kind} district's surgery is — that is how NEAK publishes them. But a district can serve several settlements: when the seat goes vacant, the villages attached to it appear nowhere in a seat-based count. This section turns the question around and classifies every settlement.
coverage.servedKnown: On the GP side the registry lists which settlements each district serves, so "serves" here comes from the source.
coverage.servedUnknown: On the dental side the registry publishes only the surgery's own settlement, so "no data" here means there is no dental surgery in the settlement. That is a weaker statement and is marked separately.
coverage.lead: settlements are touched by a vacant {kind} district ({people} residents, {share} of the population) — a seat-based count would show {seats}
coverage.classPartial: Has both a filled and a vacant district
coverage.classSubtitle: The settlements of the selected group · filterable, exportable
coverage.affectedOld: residents over 65 in the affected settlements
coverage.tableSubtitle: Every settlement's state, population and age composition
coverage.countySubtitle: How many settlements and residents a vacancy touches
coverage.note: Data as of {month}. Being affected is not the same as being unserved: substitution is invisible in the published data. Age composition: KSH, 2022 census.
coverage.trendTitle: How has this moved in the archive?
coverage.trendExplain: {from}: {fromN} affected settlements — {to}: {toN}. The solid line is all affected settlements, the dashed one those served only by vacant districts.

composite.heading: Composite care-risk index
composite.explain: Each analysis answers one question: is there a physician, how far is the next surgery, how old is the population, how likely is a vacancy. Trouble is when they point the same way at once. The index is the weighted mean of eight components, computed for every settlement, and every score can be taken apart into the components that made it.
composite.caveat: This is a comparison, not a verdict: a high index means several public indicators point the same way — not that care is unavailable there. Distances are crow-flies kilometres from the settlement centre, not travel time. Every component enters as a national rank percentile so that kilometres and shares can be added at all.
composite.lead: settlements fall into the two highest bands out of {total} ({people} residents)
composite.weightsTitle: What is the index made of?
composite.weightsExplain: The weights are deliberately round numbers and are published here. Where a component has no data for a settlement it is left out of that settlement's mean rather than estimated.

component.oncallKm: Distance to a central on-call surgery
component.outpatientMin: Driving time to an outpatient site

composite.topTitle: The ten settlements with the highest index
composite.tableSubtitle: Every settlement's index and the raw values behind it
composite.countySubtitle: Mean index and the settlements in the two highest bands
composite.note: Data as of {month}. Sources: NEAK contracted providers, EESZT master publication, KSH 2022 census and gazetteer, government decree 105/2015. (IV. 23.).

age.title: Age composition: who lives there?
age.explain: A vacancy rate means something different where a third of the residents are over 65. In the {year} census {young} of the national population were 0–14 and {old} were 65 or older; the spread between counties is far larger than that.
age.tableSubtitle: The {year} census shares carried onto today's population
age.note: Source: KSH, {year} census (CC BY 4.0). The composition comes from the census shares, the headcounts are those shares applied to the population on 1 January {population}. In {suppressed} tiny settlements KSH suppressed the cell for disclosure control; those are left missing rather than estimated.

emergency.heading: On-call and ambulance: what stands around a vacant district?
emergency.explain: Until now the site could only say that a district is vacant. The other half is in the same EESZT register it downloads every month: {oncall} central on-call services and {ambulance} ambulance units with a licence and premises. So for every settlement and every district without a physician it can say how far the nearest on-call surgery and ambulance station are.
emergency.caveat: With care: distances are crow-flies, and a nearby on-call point does not prove that care arrives — nor does a distant one prove that it does not. This is a bearing, not a verdict.
emergency.median: median distance to the nearest such point ({group})
emergency.districtMedian: median distance from districts without a physician
emergency.districtsBeyond20: districts without a physician beyond 20 km
emergency.mapCount: {n} / {total} on-call and emergency points on the map
emergency.districtTitle: {kind} districts without a physician and the nearest on-call point
emergency.districtSubtitle: Every vacant and dissolved district with its nearest on-call surgery and ambulance station
emergency.settlementTitle: Settlements and the nearest on-call point
emergency.pointSubtitle: Central on-call, ambulance, patient transport and dialysis · filterable, exportable
emergency.countySubtitle: Median and largest distance, and how many residents live beyond 20 km
emergency.note: Source: EESZT master publication, {asOf}. Central on-call: {oncallLocated} of {oncallTotal} services geocoded, ambulance: {ambulanceLocated} of {ambulanceTotal}. Substitution and weekday surgery hours are invisible in the public data.

workforce.heading: Who holds the districts?
workforce.explain: Since {from} every archived month names the contracted physician of each filled {kind} district. Put side by side, {months} months show what no snapshot can: today {physicians} physicians hold the {districts} filled districts, and it is visible which district changed hands, and how often.
workforce.privacy: No name appears here: the pipeline turns every physician into a pseudonymous key before counting anything, so this block can only say how many — never who. A name is a weak identity: two physicians can share one, which is worth remembering when reading the numbers.
workforce.statMulti: physicians hold more than one district
workforce.statMultiDistricts: districts are held by a physician with several ({share})
workforce.statLargest: districts in the largest single holding
workforce.statChanged: of districts changed physician at least once
workforce.bandsTitle: How many districts does one physician hold?
workforce.bandsExplain: The bar shows the number of physicians, with the districts they hold in brackets.
workforce.portfolioSubtitle: One row per physician's pseudonymous key and the districts they hold
workforce.districtSubtitle: How often a district changed physician in the archive
workforce.countySubtitle: Where physicians change often, and where one holds several districts
workforce.note: {changes} physician changes over {months} months. {crossCounty} physicians hold districts in more than one county. The archived months are unevenly spaced, so a short change between two snapshots can stay invisible.

clusters.heading: Contiguous care deserts
clusters.explain: The composite index ranks settlements one by one, and read that way it looks like scattered bad luck. It is not: where a high-index settlement is surrounded by similar ones, the next village is no alternative either. Here the settlements of the two highest bands are joined when their centres are within {km} km; every connected patch of at least {min} settlements is a care desert.
clusters.statSettlements: settlements belong to one of them ({share})
clusters.tableSubtitle: One row per area: its size, extent and mean indicators
clusters.memberSubtitle: Which settlement belongs to which area
clusters.note: Method: single linkage at a {km} km radius, at least {min} settlements. Linkage also joins long corridors, so the extent travels beside the size in every row. Data as of {month}.

travel.heading: Driving time instead of straight lines
travel.explain: Every distance on this site has been a crow-flies kilometre — we always said so, but a number that is wrong in a known direction is still wrong. From here the same distances are free-flow driving minutes on the OpenStreetMap road network. The Cserehát and the Őrség have been flattered by every chart we have published.
travel.caveat: Not modelled: traffic, turn restrictions, ferries, seasonal closures and roads across the border. The result is a free-flow lower bound: real journeys are longer rather than shorter. Trains and buses have their own section.
travel.median: median driving time to the nearest one ({layer})
travel.detourTitle: Where does the straight line lie most?
travel.detourExplain: These settlements show the largest gap between the air distance and the road: a river, a ridge or a dead end sits in between. (In the Danube Bend and on Szentendre Island a ferry does too — which is not modelled.)
travel.tableSubtitle: Minutes, straight-line kilometres and the gap, per settlement
travel.countySubtitle: Median driving times and residents beyond 30 minutes
travel.note: Road network: OpenStreetMap (ODbL), {source}. Settlements and destinations are snapped to the nearest road node, never to a motorway — you cannot leave one where you need to.

transit.heading: Can you get there by bus?
transit.explain: Driving time answers the question for a household with a car. In the villages this site keeps pointing at, that is exactly what cannot be assumed. On an ordinary Wednesday ({day}) scheduled buses leave from {settlements} of {total} settlements — the question is whether any of them goes, without a change, to where the care is.
transit.caveat: "No direct bus" does not mean unreachable: with a change it often works. But a change is exactly what an eighty-year-old cannot always make. Trains are not in the data (MÁV releases its timetable only on request), and Budapest runs on a separate feed, so the capital's districts are left out of this section.
transit.lead: settlements have no direct bus to the nearest {target} ({people} residents)
transit.statNoService: settlements have no bus that day ({people} residents)
transit.tableSubtitle: Departures and direct services to where care is
transit.countySubtitle: Where most settlements lack a direct service
